question: At equal CURRENT usable host biomass, does randomized past exposure to an introduced larval host causally change capacity to produce flight-capable adults after its removal?

prior_art.already_established: A population adopted an introduced host and collapsed after management shifted local microclimate.
A different population retained ancestral-host competence and showed temporal preference change.

prior_art.study: Singer and Parmesan 2021 Global Change Biology 10.1111/gcb.15656
prior_art.already_established: Long-term population host-use shifts and narrowing in E. editha.
Novel lethal host can elicit heritable, sex-linked oviposition preference in Pieris macdunnoughii.

species_gate: At least two independent butterfly species with laboratory-feasible documented development on both a locally ancestral and introduced plant. Do NOT use lethally unsuitable novel hosts for multigeneration propagation.
recruitment_gate: Multiple geographically separate source populations per butterfly species; independent maternal families within populations; final sample size selected from blinded survival/variance pilot.
permissions: Only permitted laboratory/enclosure rearing; threatened/protected butterfly handling and host-plant manipulation require appropriate approvals. Do not remove natural invasive hosts experimentally without ecological safeguards.

randomization.source: Split siblings or independent maternal lines within population into randomized resource-history arms before treatment outcomes, balancing parents and batch
history_arms: Two generations with native hosts only
Two generations with both native and introduced hosts, matched initial total edible biomass
randomization.carryover_control: A common standardized pre-assay adult holding period across history arms; randomize plant pot and tester placement
randomization.assay_design: Within each randomized history arm, randomly assign replicated lines to current mixed-host condition or introduced-host-loss condition
current_arms: Retention: 50% native and 50% established introduced food biomass
Loss: 100% native host biomass (replace introduced biomass with native biomass, keeping total edible biomass constant)
controls: maternal nutritional history and larval rearing crowding
randomization.avoid: Do not select only surviving mothers and call treatment effects survival-independent; retain initial assigned lines and attrition denominators

measurements.primary: Number of flight-capable adults produced per initially assigned mated female within fixed follow-up period; zero after entire-lineage extinction counts as zero
secondary: probability of ancestral-host oviposition within first 48h
egg clustering, larval biomass, parasitoid fate
after-loss rebound in next generation if feasible
measurements.unit: maternal lineage nested in population and species, not eggs; plant and enclosure are treatment units where shared
measurements.timing: History generations G1-G2 and prospective offspring G3-G4 as feasible, without post-hoc interval selection

estimand.primary: (E[Y | history=adopted,loss] - E[Y | history=adopted,retain]) - (E[Y | history=native,loss] - E[Y | history=native,retain])
estimand.interpretation: Intention-to-treat causal interaction of randomized experimental history and randomized current composition, not a retrospective natural invasion effect
estimand.fit: Prespecified negative-binomial/hurdle mixed model after a variance/zero audit blinded to treatment outcome; report raw means and population-stratified contrasts irrespective of significance
robustness: exclude introduced-host trials with demonstrated lethal physiological toxicity only per predefined eligibility
family/block bootstrap rather than egg bootstrap
estimand.null: No history×loss interaction under matched current edible biomass
estimand.positive: Introduced-host history worsens viable offspring recovery after removal even though usable native biomass is held constant, consistently across independent populations and ideally both species
estimand.opposite: Retained fallback or increased capacity following exposure is equally informative
estimand.mechanism_limits: A 1–2-generation history effect can reflect learning or maternal carryover; do not claim heritable evolutionary change unless multigeneration common garden, pedigrees and/or reciprocal crosses identify inheritance.

feasibility_milestones: Confirm local native and introduced plants produce viable adult butterflies in multiple species
Confirm independent rearing and source identity
Freeze independent randomization and analysis before treatment
No hypothesis testing from static map in lieu of manipulation
stop_rules: If one/both host diets cannot reach flight-capable adulthood, multigeneration randomization invalid; stop or redesign and re-register
If treatment pot-stage or total edible biomass differs systematically, cannot attribute effect to history or functional fallback
If >1 species is not feasible, interpretation restricted to focal species
No cohort outcomes -> no demographic inference
No retrospective claim from short-term within-female egg-choice series
